chunks: Ibn Mahbub narrated from Hisham ibn Salim, from Ziyad ibn Suqah, from Al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'May Allah rectify you. Some people have thirty-two teeth, while others have twenty-eight. Upon how many teeth is the blood money calculated?' He said: 'The natural creation is twenty-eight teeth: twelve in the front of the mouth and sixteen in the back. Based on this, the blood money of the teeth is distributed. The blood money for each of the front teeth, if broken until it is lost, is five hundred dirhams; since there are twelve, their total blood money is six thousand dirhams. The blood money for each of the molars, if broken until it is lost, is two hundred and fifty dirhams; since there are sixteen, their total blood money is four thousand dirhams. Thus, the total blood money for both the front and back teeth is ten thousand dirhams. The blood money was set according to this, so any extra teeth beyond twenty-eight have no blood money, and any missing teeth have no blood money.'
And thus we found it in the book of the Commander of the Faithful.

Al-Hakam said: I asked, 'Wasn't blood money previously taken from camels, cows, and sheep?' He said: 'That was in the desert communities before Islam. When Islam became widespread and silver became abundant among people, the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) set it in terms of silver.'

Al-Hakam said: I asked him, 'What about those who live in the desert today? What is taken from them as blood money - silver or camels?' He said: 'Camels are equivalent to silver, rather, they are better than silver for blood money. Indeed, they used to take one hundred camels for unintentional killing, with each camel valued at one hundred dirhams, making a total of ten thousand dirhams.'
I asked: 'What are the ages of the one hundred camels?' He said: 'They must be male camels that have completed one full year.'

key_terms.الْخِلْقَةُ: Natural creation or standard biological makeup
key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money or compensation for injury/death

ai.seo_question: How is the blood money for teeth calculated in Shia jurisprudence and what is the historical basis for using silver or camels?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih* establishes the jurisprudential standard of twenty-eight teeth for *diyyah* calculations, assigning higher value to incisors (six thousand dirhams) than molars (four thousand dirhams). It highlights the historical evolution of compensation from pre-Islamic livestock to silver currency under Imam Ali, while affirming the continued validity of camels as a superior medium for blood money in desert communities.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.5304 - Ibn Mahbub narrated from Hisham ibn Salim, from Ziyad ibn Suqah, from Al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, who said: I asked Abu Jafar Imam Muhammad ibn Ali Al-Baqir (as), "May Allah rectify your affairs. Some people have thirty-two teeth in their mouths, while others have twenty-eight. Upon how many teeth is the diyyah (blood money) calculated?"

Imam (as) said: "The natural creation consists of twenty-eight teeth - twelve in the front of the mouth and sixteen in the back. The diyyah of the teeth has been distributed based on this.
The diyyah for each of the twelve front teeth, if broken and completely lost, is five hundred dirhams, making the total diyyah for them six thousand dirhams.
The diyyah for each of the sixteen molars, if broken and completely lost, is two hundred and fifty dirhams, making the total diyyah for them four thousand dirhams.
Thus, the total diyyah for both the front and back teeth amounts to ten thousand dirhams.
The diyyah has been set according to this calculation, so any extra teeth beyond twenty-eight have no diyyah, nor is there a diyyah for any missing teeth beyond this standard count."
And thus, we found it recorded in the book of Commander of the Faithful Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (as).

Al-Hakam said: I then asked, "Before today, diyyah (blood money) used to be taken from camels, cows, and sheep. What is the ruling on that?"
Imam (as) said: "That was in the desert communities before Islam. But when Islam became widespread and silver (warq) became abundant among people, Commander of the Faithful Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (as), set the diyyah in terms of silver."

Al-Hakam continued: I then asked Imam (as), "What about those who live in the desert today? What should be taken from them as diyyah - silver or camels?"
Imam (as) said: "Camels are equivalent to silver, rather, they are even better than silver for diyyah. Indeed, they used to take one hundred camels for unintentional killing (diyat Al-khata'), with each camel being valued at one hundred dirhams, making a total of ten thousand dirhams."

I asked: "What are the required ages of the one hundred camels?"
Imam (as) said: "They should all be male camels that have completed one full year."
